Analise o(s) documento(s) de cenário do projeto e gere o SRS completo no formato especificado, seguindo o processo de trabalho: buscas dedicadas na base de conhecimento para cada tipo de artefato, rastreabilidade validada entre os artefatos.

Documento(s) de cenário:
--- Project Scenario 2.pdf ---
Unified University Inventory System (UUIS)
So basically right now we've got no single way of tracking 
everything the university owns across the faculties — 
computers, furniture, software licenses, rooms, even who's 
sitting where — and it's all over the place depending on which 
department you ask. Each faculty kind of does its own thing 
with spreadsheets or whatever old system they inherited, and 
nobody at the university level can just look something up and 
trust the answer. We want to build one system that everybody 
logs into, students, staff, IT people, deans, whoever, and 
depending on who they are they can see and manage the stuff 
that's relevant to them, but it's all sitting in one place 
instead of scattered everywhere. 
 
The way I picture it, once someone logs in (and for the people 
with more access we probably want something extra like a voice 
check, not just a password) they land on a menu where they can 
look up people, assets, locations and licenses, add new ones, 
edit them, get rid of stuff that's no longer around. Nothing 
should ever really disappear though, more like get marked as 
inactive so we keep history. People should also be able to 
lump assets or rooms into groups, like all the printers on a 
floor, or split things into subgroups, and bring in old data 
from CSV files from whatever system they're using today 
instead of typing everything from scratch. 
 
There's also this whole request and approval thing that 
matters a lot to us. If someone wants to move an item, report 
something broken, or just ask for a new asset, they should be 
able to submit that and it goes up to whoever's one level 
above them to approve or deny it, and if they say no they need 
to actually explain why. The exception is the people at the 
very top, university-level admins basically, their requests 
just go through automatically since there's nobody above to 
check them. Speaking of levels, this is kind of the backbone 
of the whole thing: department, faculty, university, and then 
a base user level, and what you can see and touch depends on 
where you sit, a faculty admin can reach into all the 
departments under them but a department admin only sees their 
own patch. 
 
We also want decent search, both a quick one where you just 
type something and a more detailed one where you can filter by 
different fields and combine conditions, plus some basic 
reporting, like comparing how many chairs or computers a room 
has against its supposed capacity. And everything anyone does 
in the system needs to get logged somewhere so if there's ever 
a question about who changed what, someone with the right 
permission can pull that up. 
 
A couple more things that matter even if they're not the 
flashy part. We can't have more than about two hundred people 
hammering the system at the same time, so it needs to hold up 
under that kind of load without falling over. If nobody 
touches it for half an hour, just log them out automatically, 
we don't want sessions sitting open forever. And if something 
crashes or a connection drops halfway through someone entering 
data, whatever they hadn't saved yet needs to come back to 
them when they log back in instead of just vanishing, losing 
someone's work because the system hiccuped would be a 
nightmare. On the security side, everything going over the 
network needs to be encrypted properly, and let's put a 
CAPTCHA on anything automated so bots can't just hammer the 
login. 
 
Things like managing permissions themselves, creating new 
roles, tweaking what each role can do, that's more of an 
admin-only corner of the system and honestly not the part 
we're most excited about, it just needs to exist so the 
higher-ups can keep control. Multiple languages and that kind 
of polish, plus the heavier department and faculty specific 
functions, those can wait for a later version, we're fine if 
version one is English-only and covers the main stuff for now. 
What we really care about for this first round is getting 
people, assets, locations and licenses all visible and 
manageable in one web system that anyone in the university can 
log into through a browser without needing anything special 
installed.

Sistema: Unified University Inventory System (UUIS)

Resumo executivo: The UUIS is a browser-based university inventory system that consolidates records of people, assets, locations, software licenses, occupancy, and organizational hierarchy. It replaces fragmented faculty-level spreadsheets and legacy tools with a centralized, access-controlled repository, enabling traceable inventory administration, approval workflows, reporting, and auditability.

Escopo: The UUIS enables university users to centrally manage and search inventory-related information through a web browser according to their organizational access level.
  Em escopo: Authentication, session control, CAPTCHA, and additional voice verification for elevated-access users
  Em escopo: Role and organizational-level access control
  Em escopo: Registration, update, consultation, and inactivation of people, assets, locations, and software licenses
  Em escopo: Asset and location grouping and subgrouping
  Em escopo: CSV import of legacy inventory data
  Em escopo: Movement, fault-reporting, and new-asset request workflows
  Em escopo: Approval, denial, and automatic approval according to organizational hierarchy
  Em escopo: Quick search and advanced multi-condition search
  Em escopo: Capacity comparison reports for rooms
  Em escopo: Audit logging and audit-log consultation
  Em escopo: Administrative management of roles and permissions
  Fora de escopo: Multilingual interface — version 1 is English-only
  Fora de escopo: Department- and faculty-specific advanced functions — deferred to a later version
  Fora de escopo: Native desktop or mobile application — the system is browser-based
  Premissa: PA-01: University users have access to a supported web browser and network connectivity.
  Premissa: PA-02: Legacy data owners provide CSV files with identifiable columns for migration. [INFERRED]
  Premissa: PA-03: The university maintains an organizational hierarchy containing base user, department, faculty, and university levels. [INFERRED]
  Restrição: REST-01 (Capacity): The system must support up to 200 concurrent users.
  Restrição: REST-02 (Platform): The system must be accessible through a web browser without special software installation.
  Restrição: REST-03 (Language): Version 1 must provide its interface in English only.
  Restrição: REST-04 (Security): Network communications must be encrypted.
  Restrição: REST-05 (Session): Inactive user sessions must expire after 30 minutes.

Stakeholders:
  STK-01 - Base user (student or staff member) (Usuário primário): Access authorized records and submit inventory movement, fault, and new-asset requests.
  STK-02 - Department administrator (Usuário primário): Manage records within the assigned department and approve requests from users one organizational level below.
  STK-03 - Faculty administrator (Usuário primário): Manage and consult records across departments belonging to the assigned faculty.
  STK-04 - University administrator (Usuário primário): Manage university-wide records, roles, permissions, audit records, and automatically processed administrator requests.
  STK-05 - IT staff member (Usuário primário): Register, update, search, and monitor information about technology assets and software licenses within authorized scope.
  STK-06 - Dean (Usuário secundário): Consult faculty-level inventory information and capacity comparison reports.
  STK-07 - University audit authority (Stakeholder externo): Consult authorized audit records to identify who performed inventory-related actions.

Regras de negócio:
  RN-001 - Organizational hierarchy: The university organizational hierarchy consists of base user, department, faculty, and university levels.
  RN-002 - Hierarchical visibility: An administrator may access records within the organizational units below the administrator's assigned level; department administrators are limited to their own department.
  RN-003 - Preservation of historical records: Inventory-related records that are no longer active must remain historically available and be identified as inactive rather than removed.
  RN-004 - Request approval routing: A movement, fault-reporting, or new-asset request must be decided by an authorized user one organizational level above the requester.
  RN-005 - Denial justification: Every denied request must include a justification supplied by the denying approver.
  RN-006 - Audit accountability: Actions performed on university inventory information must be attributable to the user who performed them.

Requisitos funcionais:
  RF-001 - Password authentication: The system must authenticate a registered user using valid credentials. [Must have]
  RF-002 - Elevated-access voice verification: The system must request voice verification after credential authentication for users assigned elevated access. [INFERRED] [Should have]
  RF-003 - Role-based authorization: The system must authorize each requested operation according to the authenticated user's role and organizational level. [Must have]
  RF-004 - Register person: The system must register a person record within the user's authorized organizational scope. [Must have]
  RF-005 - Update person: The system must update an existing person record within the user's authorized organizational scope. [Must have]
  RF-006 - Inactivate person: The system must mark a person record as inactive without removing its historical record. [Must have]
  RF-007 - Register asset: The system must register an asset record within the user's authorized organizational scope. [Must have]
  RF-008 - Update asset: The system must update an existing asset record within the user's authorized organizational scope. [Must have]
  RF-009 - Inactivate asset: The system must mark an asset record as inactive without removing its historical record. [Must have]
  RF-010 - Register location: The system must register a location record within the user's authorized organizational scope. [Must have]
  RF-011 - Update location: The system must update an existing location record within the user's authorized organizational scope. [Must have]
  RF-012 - Inactivate location: The system must mark a location record as inactive without removing its historical record. [Must have]
  RF-013 - Register software license: The system must register a software license record within the user's authorized organizational scope. [Must have]
  RF-014 - Update software license: The system must update an existing software license record within the user's authorized organizational scope. [Must have]
  RF-015 - Inactivate software license: The system must mark a software license record as inactive without removing its historical record. [Must have]
  RF-016 - Manage groups: The system must create groups and subgroups for assets or locations. [Should have]
  RF-017 - Import CSV data: The system must import people, asset, location, and software-license records from a CSV file. [Must have]
  RF-018 - Quick search: The system must return authorized people, assets, locations, and software-license records matching a user-entered search term. [Must have]
  RF-019 - Advanced search: The system must return authorized records matching combined field-based filter conditions. [Should have]
  RF-020 - Submit inventory request: The system must submit a request classified as asset movement, fault report, or new-asset request. [Must have]
  RF-021 - Route request for approval: The system must route a submitted request to an authorized approver one organizational level above the requester. [Must have]
  RF-022 - Approve request: The system must record an approver's approval decision for a request routed to that approver. [Must have]
  RF-023 - Deny request: The system must record an approver's denial decision only when a justification is provided. [Must have]
  RF-024 - Automatically approve university administrator request: The system must assign approved status to a request submitted by a university administrator. [Must have]
  RF-025 - Generate capacity comparison report: The system must generate a report comparing the quantity of chairs or computers assigned to a location with that location's recorded capacity. [Should have]
  RF-026 - Record audit event: The system must record the authenticated user, action, affected record, and timestamp for each inventory-related operation. [Must have]
  RF-027 - Consult audit log: The system must display audit events to a user authorized to consult audit records. [Must have]
  RF-028 - Manage roles and permissions: The system must allow a university administrator to create roles and configure the operations permitted for each role. [Must have]

Requisitos não funcionais:
  RNF-001 (Performance Efficiency) - The system must complete 95% of authenticated search and record-consultation requests within 2 seconds while 200 concurrent users are active. [TBD] | Métrica: 95th-percentile response time of 2 seconds or less with 200 concurrent simulated users.
  RNF-002 (Security) - The system must invalidate an authenticated session after 30 consecutive minutes without user activity. | Métrica: 100% of tested sessions are invalidated between 30 and 31 minutes of inactivity.
  RNF-003 (Security) - The system must encrypt 100% of client-server communications using TLS 1.2 or higher. [TBD: confirm minimum protocol version] | Métrica: 100% of externally accessible connections use TLS 1.2 or higher; connections using lower versions are rejected.
  RNF-004 (Security) - The system must require a successful CAPTCHA validation before processing each automated authentication attempt. [TBD: define automated-attempt detection rule] | Métrica: 100% of authentication attempts classified as automated are rejected unless CAPTCHA validation succeeds.
  RNF-005 (Reliability) - The system must restore unsaved data-entry content to the authenticated user after a connection loss or application failure followed by a new login. [TBD: confirm retained fields and retention period] | Métrica: 100% of test interruptions restore all entered field values that were not explicitly discarded.
  RNF-006 (Compatibility) - The system must execute core version-1 functions in Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari without requiring client-side software installation. [TBD: confirm supported browser versions] | Métrica: Zero critical failures across registration, search, request submission, and approval tests in the four supported browser families.

Casos de uso:

    1. The actor enters credentials.
    2. The system validates the credentials.
    3. The system establishes an authenticated session.
  UC-002 - Register asset | Ator: IT staff member
    1. The actor selects asset registration.
    2. The system displays the asset-registration form.
    3. The actor enters asset data and submits the form.
    4. The system records the asset and its audit event.
  UC-003 - Import legacy data | Ator: University administrator
    1. The actor selects CSV import.
    2. The system requests a CSV file.
    3. The actor uploads a CSV file.
    4. The system imports valid records and records audit events.
  UC-004 - Search inventory records | Ator: Base user
    1. The actor enters a search term.
    2. The system searches authorized people, assets, locations, and license records.
    3. The system displays matching authorized records.
  UC-005 - Submit inventory request | Ator: Base user
    1. The actor selects a request type.
    2. The system displays the corresponding request form.
    3. The actor submits the request.
    4. The system records the request and routes it to the next organizational level.
  UC-006 - Decide inventory request | Ator: Department administrator
    1. The actor opens a routed request.
    2. The system displays the request details.
    3. The actor selects approval.
    4. The system records approved status and an audit event.
  UC-007 - Generate capacity comparison report | Ator: Dean
    1. The actor selects a location.
    2. The system retrieves the location capacity and assigned asset quantities.
    3. The system displays the capacity comparison report.
  UC-008 - Consult audit log | Ator: University audit authority
    1. The actor opens the audit log.
    2. The system retrieves authorized audit events.
    3. The system displays the user, action, affected record, and timestamp for each event.

  CA-006 - Dado an active person record, quando an authorized administrator inactivates the record, então the system retains the record and sets its status to inactive
  CA-007 - Dado an authorized IT staff member, quando the staff member submits valid asset data, então the system creates one active asset record
  CA-008 - Dado an existing asset in authorized scope, quando an authorized user submits an updated asset value, então the system stores the updated value in that asset record
  CA-009 - Dado an active asset record, quando an authorized user inactivates it, então the system retains the asset record and sets its status to inactive
  CA-010 - Dado an authorized administrator, quando the administrator submits valid location data, então the system creates one active location record
  CA-011 - Dado an existing authorized location, quando an authorized administrator submits updated location data, então the system stores the updated values in the location record
  CA-012 - Dado an active location record, quando an authorized administrator inactivates it, então the system retains the location record and sets its status to inactive
  CA-013 - Dado an authorized IT staff member, quando the staff member submits valid software-license data, então the system creates one active software-license record
  CA-014 - Dado an existing authorized software-license record, quando an authorized user submits updated license data, então the system stores the updated values in the license record
  CA-015 - Dado an active software-license record, quando an authorized user inactivates it, então the system retains the license record and sets its status to inactive
  CA-016 - Dado an authorized faculty administrator, quando the administrator creates a subgroup under an existing asset group, então the system stores the subgroup linked to its parent group
  CA-017 - Dado a valid CSV file containing asset records, quando a university administrator uploads the file, então the system registers each valid asset record from the file
  CA-018 - Dado an authenticated user authorized to view a matching asset, quando the user enters a matching search term, então the system displays the matching asset record
  CA-019 - Dado an authenticated IT staff member, quando the staff member submits two combined field filters, então the system displays only authorized records satisfying both filters
  CA-020 - Dado an authenticated base user, quando the user submits a request classified as fault report, então the system creates one request with type fault report
  CA-021 - Dado a request submitted by a base user assigned to a department, quando the request is created, então the system assigns the request to an authorized approver one organizational level above the requester
  CA-022 - Dado a request routed to an authorized approver, quando the approver selects approval, então the system sets the request status to approved
  CA-023 - Dado a request routed to an authorized approver, quando the approver selects denial without a justification, então the system does not record the denial and displays a justification-required message
  CA-024 - Dado a request submitted by a university administrator, quando the administrator submits the request, então the system creates the request with status approved without assigning an approver
  CA-025 - Dado a location with recorded capacity and assigned chair quantities, quando an authorized dean generates the location report, então the system displays the recorded capacity and assigned chair quantity
  CA-026 - Dado an authenticated user successfully updates an asset, quando the update is completed, então the system records one audit event containing the user, action, affected asset, and timestamp
  CA-027 - Dado a user with audit-log permission and an existing audit event, quando the user opens the audit log, então the system displays the event with user, action, affected record, and timestamp
  CA-028 - Dado an authenticated university administrator, quando the administrator creates a role and assigns an operation permission, então the system stores the role with the assigned operation permission

Glossário:
  Asset: A university-owned item tracked by the UUIS, such as a computer, chair, printer, or furniture item.
  Software license: A record representing the university's right to use a software product.
  Location: A room or other physical university space to which assets or people may be associated.
  Organizational scope: The university, faculty, department, or subordinate units whose records a user is authorized to access.
  Inactive record: A historical record that is retained in the system but is no longer considered active.
  Inventory request: A request for asset movement, fault reporting, or acquisition of a new asset.
  Elevated access: Access assigned to users with broader administrative permissions requiring additional voice verification. [INFERRED]
  Audit event: A traceable record of an inventory-related action performed by an authenticated user.

Este documento é a base de conhecimento fixa (Vector Store B) do sistema de elicitação de requisitos. Ele ensina ao agente

Base: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 §9.6 · IEEE 830-1998 §3 · Sommerville (2016, cap. 4)
O Documento de Especificação de Requisitos de Software (SRS) é o contrato técnico que descreve o 
que o sistema deve fazer e sob quais condições de qualidade. Ele serve de referência para 
desenvolvedores, testadores, gerentes e clientes durante todo o ciclo de vida do projeto.
1.1 Artefatos Obrigatórios e sua Ordem
Um SRS completo e formal deve conter os seguintes artefatos, nesta ordem:
• ESCOPO: Define o que está DENTRO e FORA do projeto. Evita scope creep.
• STAKEHOLDERS: Lista todos os envolvidos: quem usa, quem financia, quem é afetado.
• PREMISSAS E RESTRIÇÕES: Fatos assumidos como verdadeiros e limites impostos ao projeto.
• REGRAS DE NEGÓCIO (RN): Políticas, fórmulas e condições de negócio que existem independentemente 
do software.
• REQUISITOS FUNCIONAIS (RF): O que o sistema DEVE FAZER — comportamentos, serviços, respostas a 
entradas.
• REQUISITOS NÃO FUNCIONAIS (RNF): Como o sistema deve SER — atributos de qualidade 
quantificáveis.
• HISTÓRIAS DE USUÁRIO (HU): Necessidades na perspectiva do usuário: Como [perfil], quero [ação], para
[benefício].
• CASOS DE USO (UC): Interações detalhadas ator-sistema com fluxo principal, alternativo e exceções.
• CRITÉRIOS DE ACEITE (CA): Condições testáveis em formato BDD (Dado/Quando/Então) que definem 
quando o requisito está concluído.
• GLOSSÁRIO: Termos do domínio com definição precisa para eliminar ambiguidades.
1.2 Como os Artefatos se Interconectam
Os artefatos formam uma cadeia de rastreabilidade. Cada RF deve ter origem em um STK 
(stakeholder) ou RN. Cada HU deve ter pelo menos um RF associado. Cada RF e HU devem ter pelo menos um CA. Esta rastreabilidade garante que nada seja implementado sem justificativa de 
negócio e que tudo que foi prometido seja testável.
Cadeia de rastreabilidade mínima:
STK → (RN →) RF → HU → CA

A ISO/IEC 25010:2023 define 9 características de qualidade do produto. Todo RNF deve ser 
classificado em uma dessas características. A seguir, cada característica com seus sub-atributos e 
exemplo de RNF.
1. Functional Suitability (Adequação Funcional)
 Functional Completeness — o sistema oferece todas as funções necessárias.
 Functional Correctness — as funções produzem os resultados corretos.
 Functional Appropriateness — as funções facilitam a realização das tarefas.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 1. Functional Suitability
O sistema deve calcular o imposto sobre o valor do pedido aplicando corretamente a alíquota de ICMS 
vigente para o estado de destino, conforme tabela oficial CONFAZ, com variação máxima de R$ 0,01 em 
relação ao valor de referência da Receita Estadual.
2. Performance Efficiency (Eficiência de Desempenho)
 Time Behaviour — tempo de resposta e throughput.
 Resource Utilisation — uso de CPU, memória, rede.
 Capacity — limites máximos suportados.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 2. Performance Efficiency
O sistema deve processar no mínimo 200 pedidos por minuto sob carga de 1.000 usuários simultâneos, com 
tempo de resposta inferior a 2 segundos no percentil 95.
3. Compatibility (Compatibilidade)
 Co-existence — coexiste com outros sistemas sem degradação.
 Interoperability — troca dados com outros sistemas.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 3. Compatibility
A API do sistema deve expor endpoints REST/JSON compatíveis com o padrão OpenAPI 3.0, permitindo 
integração com o ERP legado via OAuth 2.0 sem modificações no ERP.4. Interaction Capability (Capacidade de Interação) — antes 'Usabilidade'
 Appropriateness Recognisability — usuário reconhece a adequação do sistema.
 Learnability — facilidade de aprendizado.
 Operability — facilidade de operação.
 User Error Protection — proteção contra erros do usuário.
 User Engagement — interface envolvente e motivadora.
 Inclusivity — acessível a pessoas com diferentes capacidades.
 User Assistance — suporte ao usuário.
 Self-Descriptiveness — interface autoexplicativa.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 4. Interaction Capability
Um usuário sem treinamento prévio deve ser capaz de registrar seu primeiro pedido completo em até 10 
minutos. A interface deve seguir as diretrizes WCAG 2.1 nível AA.
5. Reliability (Confiabilidade)
 Faultlessness — ausência de falhas em condições normais.
 Availability — proporção de tempo em que o sistema está operacional.
 Fault Tolerance — operação correta mesmo com falhas parciais.
 Recoverability — recuperação após falha.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 5. Reliability
O sistema deve ter disponibilidade mínima de 99,5% ao mês (máx. 3,6h de downtime não planejado). Em 
caso de falha crítica, o sistema deve restaurar a operação normal em até 4 horas (RTO = 4h).

Unified University Inventory System (UUIS)
So basically right now we've got no single way of tracking 
everything the university owns across the faculties — 
computers, furniture, software licenses, rooms, even who's 
sitting where — and it's all over the place depending on which 
department you ask. Each faculty kind of does its own thing 
with spreadsheets or whatever old system they inherited, and 
nobody at the university level can just look something up and 
trust the answer. We want to build one system that everybody 
logs into, students, staff, IT people, deans, whoever, and 
depending on who they are they can see and manage the stuff 
that's relevant to them, but it's all sitting in one place 
instead of scattered everywhere. 
The way I picture it, once someone logs in (and for the people 
with more access we probably want something extra like a voice 
check, not just a password) they land on a menu where they can 
look up people, assets, locations and licenses, add new ones, 
edit them, get rid of stuff that's no longer around. Nothing 
should ever really disappear though, more like get marked as 
inactive so we keep history. People should also be able to 
lump assets or rooms into groups, like all the printers on a 
floor, or split things into subgroups, and bring in old data 
from CSV files from whatever system they're using today 
instead of typing everything from scratch. 
There's also this whole request and approval thing that 
matters a lot to us. If someone wants to move an item, report 
something broken, or just ask for a new asset, they should be 
able to submit that and it goes up to whoever's one level 
above them to approve or deny it, and if they say no they need 
to actually explain why. The exception is the people at the 
very top, university-level admins basically, their requests 
just go through automatically since there's nobody above to 
check them. Speaking of levels, this is kind of the backbone 
of the whole thing: department, faculty, university, and then 
a base user level, and what you can see and touch depends on 
where you sit, a faculty admin can reach into all the 
departments under them but a department admin only sees their 
own patch. We also want decent search, both a quick one where you just 
type something and a more detailed one where you can filter by 
different fields and combine conditions, plus some basic 
reporting, like comparing how many chairs or computers a room 
has against its supposed capacity. And everything anyone does 
in the system needs to get logged somewhere so if there's ever 
a question about who changed what, someone with the right 
permission can pull that up. 
A couple more things that matter even if they're not the 
flashy part. We can't have more than about two hundred people 
hammering the system at the same time, so it needs to hold up 
under that kind of load without falling over. If nobody 
touches it for half an hour, just log them out automatically, 
we don't want sessions sitting open forever. And if something 
crashes or a connection drops halfway through someone entering 
data, whatever they hadn't saved yet needs to come back to 
them when they log back in instead of just vanishing, losing 
someone's work because the system hiccuped would be a 
nightmare. On the security side, everything going over the 
network needs to be encrypted properly, and let's put a 
CAPTCHA on anything automated so bots can't just hammer the 
login.

Which requirements should you specify?
It’s not always worth taking the time to generate a complete set of requirements for an entire 
production system. Many options lie between the two extremes of continuing forever with no 
requirements documentation and reconstructing a perfect requirements set. Knowing why you’d like 
to have written requirements available lets you judge whether the cost of rebuilding all—or even 
part—of the specification is a sound investment.

Rarely do you need to document the entire existing system. Focus detailed requirements efforts 
on the changes needed to meet the business objectives. If you’re replacing a system, start by 
documenting the areas prioritized as most important to achieve the business objectives or those that 
pose the highest implementation risk. Any new requirements identified during the gap analysis will 
need to be specified at the same level of precision and using the same techniques as you would for a 
new system.
Level of detail
One of the biggest challenges is determining the appropriate level of detail at which to document 
requirements gleaned from the existing system. For enhancements, defining requirements for the 
new functionality alone might be sufficient. However, you will usually benefit from documenting all of 
the functionality that closely relates to the enhancement, to ensure that the change fits in seamlessly 
(region B in Figure 21-2). You might want to create business processes, user requirements, and/or 
functional requirements for those related areas. For example, let’s say you are adding a discount code 
feature to an existing shopping cart function, but you don’t have any documented requirements for 
the shopping cart. You might be tempted to write just a single user story: “As a customer, I need to be 
able to enter a discount code so I can get the cheapest price for the product.” However, this user story 
alone lacks context, so consider capturing other user stories about shopping cart operations. That 
information could be valuable the next time you need to modify the shopping cart function.

revenue generator for at least 10 years. They also planned to reuse some of the core requirements 
in several spin-off products. In this case, it made sense to improve the requirements documentation 
for version 1 because it was the foundation for all subsequent development work in this product line.

version. Nowhere was there a description of the original system. Consequently, everyone had a 
different understanding of the current system’s capabilities. If you’re in this situation, document

Expected challenges
The presence of an existing system leads to common challenges that both enhancement and 
replacement projects will face, including the following:
■ The changes made could degrade the performance to which users are accustomed.
■ Little or no requirements documentation might be available for the existing system.
■ Users who are familiar with how the system works today might not like the changes they are 
about to encounter.
■ You might unknowingly break or omit functionality that is vital to some stakeholder group.
■ Stakeholders might take this opportunity to request new functionality that seems like a good 
idea but isn’t really needed to meet the business objectives.
Even if there is existing documentation, it might not prove useful. For enhancement projects, 
the documentation might not be up to date. If the documentation doesn’t match the existing 
application’s reality, it is of limited use. For replacement systems, you also need to be wary of carrying 
forward all of the requirements, because some of the old functionality probably should not be 
migrated.
One of the major issues in replacement projects is validating that the reasons for the replacement 
are sound. There need to be justifiable business objectives for the change. When existing systems 
are being completely replaced, organizational processes might also have to change, which makes it 
harder for people to accept a new system. The change in business processes, change in the software 
system, and learning curve of a new system can disrupt current operations.

If developers build exactly what 
customers initially request, they’ll probably have to build it again because customers often don’t 
know what they really need. In addition, the BAs might not be talking to the right people or asking 
the right questions.
The features that users present as their “wants” don’t necessarily equate to the functionality they 
need to perform their tasks with the new product. To gain a more accurate view of user needs, the 
business analyst must collect a wide range of user input, analyze and clarify it, and specify just what 
needs to be built to let users do their jobs. The BA has the lead responsibility for recording the new 
system’s necessary capabilities and properties and for communicating that information to other 
stakeholders. This is an iterative process that takes time. If you don’t invest the time to achieve this 
shared understanding—this common vision of the intended product—the certain outcomes are 
rework, missed deadlines, cost overruns, and customer dissatisfaction.
User classes
People often talk about “the user” for a software system as though all users belong to a monolithic 
group with similar characteristics and needs. In reality, most products of any size appeal to a diversity 
of users with different expectations and goals. Rather than thinking of “the user” in singular, spend 
some time identifying the multiple user classes and their roles and privileges for your product.
Classifying users
Chapter 2 described many of the types of stakeholders that a project might have. As shown in 
Figure 6-1, a user class is a subset of the product’s users, which is a subset of the product’s customers, 
which is a subset of its stakeholders. An individual can belong to multiple user classes. For example, 
an application’s administrator might also interact with it as an ordinary user at times. A product’s 
users might differ—among other ways—in the following respects, and you can group users into a 
number of distinct user classes based on these sorts of differences:
■ Their access privilege or security levels (such as ordinary user, guest user, administrator)
■ The tasks they perform during their business operations
■ The features they use
■ The frequency with which they use the product
■ Their application domain experience and computer systems expertise
■ The platforms they will be using (desktop PCs, laptop PCs, tablets, smartphones, specialized 
devices)CHAPTER 6 Finding the voice of the user 103
■ Their native language
■ Whether they will interact with the system directly or indirectly
FIGURE 6-1 A hierarchy of stakeholders, customers, users, and user classes.
It’s tempting to group users into classes based on their geographical location or the kind of 
company they work in. One company that creates software used in the banking industry initially 
considered distinguishing users based on whether they worked in a large commercial bank, a small 
commercial bank, a savings and loan institution, or a credit union. These distinctions really represent 
different market segments, though, not different user classes.
A better way to identify user classes is to think about the tasks that various users will perform with 
the system. All of those types of financial institutions will have tellers, employees who process loan 
applications, business bankers, and so forth. The individuals who perform such activities—whether 
they are job titles or simply roles—will have similar functional needs for the system across all of the 
financial institutions. Tellers all have to do more or less the same things, business bankers do more or 
less the same things, and so on. More logical user class names for a banking system therefore might 
include teller, loan officer, business banker, and branch manager. You might discover additional user 
classes by thinking of possible use cases, user stories, and process flows and who might perform them.

Prioritizing by using business objectives
Enhancement projects are undertaken to add new capabilities to an existing application. It’s easy 
to get caught up in the excitement and start adding unnecessary capabilities. To combat this risk 
of gold-plating, trace requirements back to business objectives to ensure that the new features are 
needed and to select the highest-impact features to implement first. You also might need to prioritize 
enhancement requests against the correction of defects that had been reported against the old 
system.
Also be wary of letting unnecessary new functionality slip into replacement projects. The main 
focus of replacement projects is to migrate existing functionality. However, customers might imagine 
that if you are developing a new system anyway, it is easy to add lots of new capabilities right away. 
Many replacement projects have collapsed because of the weight of uncontrolled scope growth. 
You’re usually better off building a stable first release and adding more features through subsequent 
enhancement projects, provided the first release allows users to do their jobs.
Replacement projects often originate when stakeholders want to add functionality to an existing 
system that is too inflexible to support the growth or has technology limitations. However, there needs 
to be a clear business objective to justify implementing an expensive new system (Devine 2008). Use 
the anticipated cost savings from a new system (such as through reduced maintenance of an old, 
clunky system) plus the value of the new desired functionality to justify a system replacement project.
Also look for existing functionality that doesn’t need to be retained in a replacement system. Don’t 
replicate the existing system’s shortcomings or miss an opportunity to update a system to suit new 
business needs and processes. For example, the BA might ask users, “Do you use <a particular menu 
option>?” If you consistently hear “I never do that,” then maybe it isn’t needed in the replacement 
system. Look for usage data that shows what screens, functions, or data entities are rarely accessed 
in the current system. Even the existing functionality has to map to current and anticipated business 
objectives to warrant re-implementing it in the new system.
Trap Don’t let stakeholders get away with saying “I have it today, so I need it in the new 
system” as a default method of justifying requirements.
Mind the gap
A gap analysis is a comparison of functionality between an existing system and a desired new system. 
A gap analysis can be expressed in different ways, including use cases, user stories, or features. When 
enhancing an existing system, perform a gap analysis to make sure you understand why it isn’t 
currently meeting your business objectives.
Gap analysis for a replacement project entails understanding existing functionality and discovering 
the desired new functionality (see Figure 21-1). Identify user requirements for the existing system that 
stakeholders want to have re-implemented in the new system. Also, elicit new user requirements that 
the existing system does not address. Consider any change requests that were never implemented CHAPTER 21 Enhancement and replacement projects 397
in the existing system. Prioritize the existing user requirements and the new ones together. Prioritize 
closing the gaps using business objectives as described in the previous section or the other 
prioritization techniques presented in Chapter 16, “First things first: Setting requirement priorities.”
FIGURE 21-1 When you are replacing an existing system, some requirements will be implemented unchanged, 
some will be modified, some will be discarded, and some new requirements might be added.
Maintaining performance levels
Existing systems set user expectations for performance and throughput. Stakeholders almost 
always have key performance indicators (KPIs) for existing processes that they will want to maintain 
in the new system.

- The system must track computers, furniture, software licenses, rooms, and occupants across university faculties.
- All user types (students, staff, IT people, deans) log into one system, with access scoped to what's relevant to them.
- Login for higher-access users requires an extra verification step (voice check), not just a password.
- Users can look up, add, and edit people, assets, locations, and licenses.
- Deleted records are not removed, only marked inactive, to preserve history.
- Assets and rooms can be grouped and split into subgroups.
- The system supports importing legacy data from CSV files.
- Requests to move an item, report something broken, or ask for a new asset go to the approver one level above the requester.
- Rejected requests require an explanation from the approver.
- University-level admin requests are automatically approved, since there is no approver above them.
- The access hierarchy has four levels: department, faculty, university, and base user.
- A faculty admin can access all departments under their faculty; a department admin only sees their own department.
- The system supports both a quick search and an advanced/filtered search with combinable conditions.
- Basic reporting includes comparing a room's capacity against its actual chairs/computers.
- All user actions in the system must be logged for audit purposes.
- The system must support at least 200 concurrent users.
- Sessions must time out automatically after 30 minutes of inactivity.
- Unsaved data must be recoverable without loss if a session or connection is interrupted.
- Network communication must be encrypted (SSL).
- Automated/bot actions must be blocked using CAPTCHA.
- Permission and role management is an admin-only feature.
- Version 1 is English-only; multi-language support and deeper department/faculty-specific functions are deferred to a later version.
- The system must be a browser-based web application requiring no special software installation.

casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: An authenticated session is established with the user's authorized access scope.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor enters credentials.
2. The system validates the credentials.
3. The system establishes an authenticated session.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. The actor has elevated access → the system requests voice verification; returns to step 3 after successful verification.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. Invalid credentials → the system rejects authentication and displays an authentication-failure message (ref. RF-001).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The actor is authenticated and authorized to register assets in the selected organizational scope.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: A new active asset record exists in the selected organizational scope.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor selects asset registration.
2. The system displays the asset-registration form.
3. The actor enters asset data and submits the form.
4. The system records the asset and its audit event.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. The actor imports asset data through a CSV file → the system processes the file under RF-017.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. The actor lacks authorization → the system denies the operation (ref. RN-002, RF-003).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The actor is authenticated as a university administrator and has a CSV file.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: Valid records from the CSV file are registered in the selected organizational scope.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No invalid CSV record is registered.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor selects CSV import.
2. The system requests a CSV file.
3. The actor uploads a CSV file.
4. The system imports valid records and records audit events.
fluxos_alternativos: 4a. The file contains different supported record types → the system imports each identified type.
fluxos_excecao: 4b. A record is invalid → the system reports the invalid record and does not register it (ref. RF-017).

casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The system displays matching records within the actor's authorized scope.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor enters a search term.
2. The system searches authorized people, assets, locations, and license records.
3. The system displays matching authorized records.
fluxos_alternativos: 1a. The actor selects advanced search → the system accepts combined field-based filters under RF-019.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. No matching record exists → the system displays zero results (ref. RF-018).

casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: A request is recorded and routed for approval or automatically approved.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor selects a request type.
2. The system displays the corresponding request form.
3. The actor submits the request.
4. The system records the request and routes it to the next organizational level.
fluxos_alternativos: 4a. The requester is a university administrator → the system assigns approved status automatically.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. Required request information is absent → the system identifies the absent information and does not submit the request (ref. RF-020).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: A request is routed to the actor for decision.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The request has an approved or denied decision recorded.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor opens a routed request.
2. The system displays the request details.
3. The actor selects approval.
4. The system records approved status and an audit event.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. The actor selects denial and supplies a justification → the system records denied status and the justification.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. The actor selects denial without a justification → the system rejects the decision and requests a justification (ref. RN-005, RF-023).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The actor is authenticated and authorized to consult the selected location.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: A report displays the location capacity and quantities of chairs or computers assigned to it.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No unauthorized location data is displayed.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor selects a location.
2. The system retrieves the location capacity and assigned asset quantities.
3. The system displays the capacity comparison report.
fluxos_alternativos: 1a. The actor selects another authorized location → the system regenerates the report for that location.
fluxos_excecao: 1b. The actor selects an unauthorized location → the system denies report generation (ref. RN-002, RF-025).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The actor is authenticated and has audit-log consultation permission.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The system displays authorized audit events.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No audit event is displayed to an unauthorized actor.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor opens the audit log.
2. The system retrieves authorized audit events.
3. The system displays the user, action, affected record, and timestamp for each event.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. The actor applies authorized filters → the system displays matching audit events.
fluxos_excecao: 1b. The actor lacks audit permission → the system denies access (ref. RF-003, RF-027).

Department admin — sees and manages only their own department's data; approves requests from base users below them.
Faculty admin — sees and manages all departments under their faculty; login requires an extra verification step (voice check).
University-level admin — top of the hierarchy; their requests are approved automatically, since there is no approver above them; manages permissions and roles.

regras_de_negocio.descricao: Higher-access users (department, faculty, and university admins) require an extra verification step (voice check) at login, in addition to a password.

Requests to move an item, report something broken, or request a new asset go to the approver exactly one level above the requester.
Rejected requests require an explanation from the approver.
Requests from university-level admins are automatically approved, since there is no approver above them.
A faculty admin can access all departments in their faculty; a department admin only sees their own department.
Permission and role management is an admin-only feature.

historias_de_usuario.descricao: As a base user (student/staff), I want to log in and see only what's relevant to me, so that I can manage my own view of the inventory without irrelevant data.
As a higher-access user, I want to complete an extra verification step (voice check) at login, so that my elevated access is protected beyond just a password.
As a user, I want to look up, add, and edit people, assets, locations, and licenses, so that the inventory stays up to date.
As a user, I want to submit a request to move an item, report something broken, or request a new asset, so that the right approver can review it.
As an approver, I want to approve or reject requests from users one level below me, explaining any rejection, so that the requester understands the decision.
As a department admin, I want to see and manage only my own department's data, so that I don't interfere with other departments.
As a faculty admin, I want to see and manage all departments in my faculty, so that I have full oversight of it.
As a user, I want to search using quick search or advanced/filtered search, so that I can find records efficiently.
As a user with reporting access, I want to compare a room's capacity against its actual chairs/computers, so that I can identify discrepancies.
As an admin, I want to manage permissions and roles, so that I can control what each role is allowed to access.

casos_de_uso.descricao: Submit and approve request — a user submits a request (move item/report broken/new asset), the system routes it to the approver one level above, who approves or rejects it with an explanation (or it is auto-approved if the requester is a university-level admin).
Search inventory — a user performs a quick or advanced/filtered search across people, assets, locations, and licenses.
Import legacy data — an admin imports historical inventory data from a CSV file.
Generate room capacity report — a user runs a report comparing a room's stated capacity against its actual chairs/computers.
Manage roles and permissions — an admin creates or edits roles and adjusts what each role can access.

criterios_de_aceite.descricao: Given a higher-access user attempting to log in, when they enter their password, then the system requires an additional voice verification before granting access.
Given a user submits a request, when it is sent, then the system routes it to the approver exactly one level above the requester.
Given a university-level admin submits a request, when it is sent, then the system approves it automatically, without requiring further approval.
Given 200 concurrent users accessing the system, when they perform normal operations, then the system remains responsive without failing.
Given a user session with no activity, when 30 minutes pass, then the system automatically ends the session.
